topic: Reddi Kingdoms of Kondavidu & Rajahmundry (with the Gajapatis)

items.question: Assess the role of the Reddi kingdom of Kondavidu in the political and cultural revival of Andhra in the 14th and 15th centuries.
items.modelAnswer:
After the **fall of the Kakatiyas in 1323** and the collapse of Tughluq authority, the Telugu country fragmented among three warrior lineages — the **Musunuri Nayakas**, the **Recherla Velamas** and the **Reddis**. Of these, the **Reddi kingdom of Kondavidu (c.1325–1448)**, founded by **Prolaya Vema Reddi** of the Panta clan, proved the most durable agent of political and cultural revival in coastal and central Andhra.

**Political revival.** From an initial base at **Addanki**, the Reddis restored order between the Krishna and Godavari and built a defensible state around the great hill-forts of **Kondavidu** and **Kondapalli**, to which **Anavota Reddi** moved the capital. At its peak the kingdom reached from **Cuttack to Kanchi**, with **Srisailam** to the west, and a subsidiary line at **Rajahmundry** (from 1395) extended Reddi power into the Godavari delta. Administration ran on **Dharmasutra** norms with a light **one-sixth** land tax, and the abolition of customs duties revived maritime trade through the port of **Motupalli**.

**Cultural and religious revival.** The Reddis were **champions of Hindu revival** against the disruption of the invasions — restoring Brahmin **agraharas**, endowing **Srisailam, Tirumala and Ahobilam**, and (under Prolaya Vema Reddi, 'Apratima-Bhudana-Parasurama') building the Srisailam steps and many Siva temples. Their court became a **golden age of Telugu literature**: **Errana**, the third of the Kavitraya, completed the **Aranya Parva** of the Mahabharata under Prolaya Vema Reddi, while **Srinatha**, 'Kavi Sarvabhauma', served as Vidyadhikari at Kondavidu; even kings such as **Kumaragiri Reddi** (Vasantarajiyam) were scholars.

**Conclusion.** Though finally overwhelmed — Kondavidu falling to **Vijayanagara (1424)** and Rajahmundry to the **Gajapatis (c.1448)** — the Reddis bridged the Kakatiya and Vijayanagara ages, preserving Telugu political identity, temple culture and classical literature, and so hold an honoured place in Andhra history.
keyPoints: Context: fall of Kakatiyas (1323); rise of Musunuris, Velamas and Reddis; Reddis the most durable.
Prolaya Vema Reddi (Panta clan) founded the kingdom c.1325; Addanki → Kondavidu (Anavota Reddi).
State-building: forts Kondavidu/Kondapalli, extent Cuttack–Kanchi–Srisailam, Rajahmundry branch (1395).
Economy: Dharmasutra rule, one-sixth tax, customs abolished, Motupalli sea trade.
Hindu revival: agraharas, Srisailam steps and Mallikarjuna repairs, Ahobilam, Tirumala patronage.
Literary golden age: Errana (Aranya Parva), Srinatha (Kavi Sarvabhauma), Kumaragiri (Vasantarajiyam).
Decline: Kondavidu to Vijayanagara (1424), Rajahmundry to Gajapatis (c.1448).
items.source: Wikipedia — Reddy Kingdom; History & Culture of the Andhras (Telugu Akademi / APPSC reference)

items.question: Trace the rise of the Telugu warrior powers after the fall of the Kakatiyas and the subsequent Gajapati–Vijayanagara contest for coastal Andhra.
items.modelAnswer:
The **capture of Prataparudra II in 1323** ended Kakatiya rule and briefly placed the Telugu country under the **Delhi Sultanate**, whose grip quickly weakened. Into this vacuum rose a succession of **Telugu warrior powers** whose rivalries shaped Andhra for two centuries.

**The Musunuri Nayakas.** **Prolaya Nayaka**, claiming Kakatiya descent, issued the **Vilasa grant (c.1330)** bewailing the ruin of the land. His cousin **Kapaya Nayaka (r.1333–1368)** organised a broad rising and **recovered Warangal from the Tughluqs in 1336**, reportedly with **75 Nayakas** behind him. Weakened by Bahmani pressure, the Musunuris fell to the **Recherla Velamas in 1368**.

**The Reddis and Velamas.** In the coastal belt the **Reddis** built the kingdom of **Kondavidu** under **Prolaya Vema Reddi**, while the **Recherla Velamas** entrenched themselves in the Telangana uplands at **Rachakonda and Devarakonda**; the two were persistent rivals, the Velamas often allying with the **Bahmanis** against the Reddis.

**The Gajapati–Vijayanagara contest.** As the Reddis declined, two great powers competed for their coastal lands. **Vijayanagara annexed Kondavidu in 1424**, and the **Gajapatis of Odisha** — founded by **Kapilendra Deva in 1434** from their capital **Kataka** — pushed south, taking **Rajahmundry around 1448** and much of coastal Andhra. The contest was finally decided by **Krishnadevaraya of Vijayanagara**, whose defeat of **Gajapati Prataparudra Deva** (early 16th century) stripped the Gajapatis of their southern conquests.

**Conclusion.** From the Musunuri resistance through the Reddi–Velama rivalry to the Gajapati–Vijayanagara struggle, coastal Andhra passed through a century of shifting warrior powers before being absorbed into the Vijayanagara imperial order — a sequence central to APPSC's medieval-Andhra syllabus.
keyPoints: 1323: fall of Kakatiyas (Prataparudra II captured); brief Delhi Sultanate rule, then vacuum.
Musunuris: Prolaya Nayaka's Vilasa grant (c.1330); Kapaya Nayaka recovers Warangal (1336) with 75 Nayakas; fall to Recherla Velamas (1368).
Reddis (Kondavidu) and Recherla Velamas (Rachakonda/Devarakonda) as rival successor powers; Velama–Bahmani alliance.
Gajapatis founded by Kapilendra Deva (1434, capital Kataka); take Rajahmundry/coastal Andhra c.1448.
Krishnadevaraya defeats Gajapati Prataparudra Deva, ending Gajapati hold on coastal Andhra.
